claim: Points in the plane can have more pairs exactly one unit apart than Erdős conjectured, so his conjecture is false.
people_part: OpenAI describes the model as producing the disproof; outside experts saw an edited version of its reasoning, not its original output (Scientific American, 2026-05-21).
check_note: Nine mathematicians at universities and research institutes (Alon, Bloom, Gowers, Litt, Sawin, Shankar, Tsimerman, Wang and Wood) posted a short write-up of the counterexample, checked by people. None says they work for OpenAI; one, Daniel Litt, says OpenAI asked him to check it.
notes: Scientific American, 2026-05-21: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/ai-just-solved-an-80-year-old-erdos-problem-and-mathematicians-are-amazed . Also cited in the note on the claim 2025-06-10-altman-2026-systems-novel-insights.

problem: the share of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function that lie on the critical line
claim: At least two thirds of the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are simple and on the critical line, up from a previous record of 5/12.
announced_by: Anthropic, and Levent Alpöge and Ralph Furman on arXiv
people_part: The arXiv comment says the proof was discovered autonomously by Claude and checked and communicated by the listed authors.
check_note: Youness Lamzouri (Université de Lorraine) reached the same bound by a different method, and noted two estimates that the original paper neither states nor proves. No one outside has re-run the Lean proof; Anthropic says two experts read the paper, which is its own word.
notes: A better bound, not a whole problem, so no 'open since' year. Anthropic's page is dated 2026-08-10 and updated 2026-08-13, and gives the improvement as 41.6% to 67.2%. The paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13637 , version 1 posted 2026-08-13, version 2 2026-08-19; its comment says the proof was discovered autonomously by Claude.

problem: Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness, one of the Millennium Prize Problems
claim: A fluid that starts smooth can break down in a finite time while its energy stays finite, in the version of the problem where an outside force is applied.
ai_system: an unreleased OpenAI model, run as about 10,000 agents at once
people_part: OpenAI's page does not describe a part played by people.
check_note: Researchers at King's College London argue that the Lean version does not fully match the written proof, and say they have not shown the proof wrong. The Clay Mathematics Institute's review is under way.
notes: OpenAI's page is dated 2026-09-08 and updated 2026-09-10; about 88 hours of agent work, then 17 hours for the Lean version, made with a model OpenAI calls GPT-6 Astra; OpenAI says it will not claim the prize. Clay's statement of 2026-09-11 says the problem has apparently been settled and does not name OpenAI: https://www.claymath.org/news/navier-stokes-announcement . The objection: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08144 . A dispute over credit: Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge posted related work on the Euler equations the night before, which OpenAI's page credits.

problem: the Riemann Hypothesis, one of the Millennium Prize Problems
claim: A proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, and of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, released as Lean code.
people_part: He says he steered the work to the right setting, that Claude then far outpaced him, and that he does not yet understand parts of the argument.
check_note: Andrew Sutherland (MIT) compiled the code, and Lean's checker accepted it with only the three standard axioms. The check that the statement in Lean is the real theorem had not been reported.
notes: About 17.4 million lines of Lean, per a public mirror: https://github.com/Tomodovodoo/Riemann . The generalised version covers Dirichlet L-functions only, per the README of the mirror https://github.com/n4rr4k/riemann-hypothesis .
